beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — the ask lands answered; one output line per chapter plus the through-line.
beats.narration_text: Annyeong — I'm Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. Three chapters, three builds: where to cut a document, how to search a hundred thousand vectors, and which kind of match to trust. Each one looked like it should have a single best answer. In all three, the honest answer turned out to be the same shape.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW. The correction IS the reel's misconception: that these three are solved problems with best-practice defaults, rather than design problems with settings you pick.
beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea. These are design problems. Chunk size, recall, and which matcher to trust are all settings you choose — and in all three chapters, the convenient default did not survive contact with a measurement.

beats.act: ACT 1 — chapter four: no correct chunk size
beats.role_note: Carried verbatim from claude-rag-chunking B03. No number changed.
beats.narration_text: Chapter four: chunking. Too small, and a chunk loses the context that gave it meaning — five days per year, five days of what? Too large, and one fact gets diluted among everything around it. The chapter refuses to name a correct size, and it is right to. The axis has two failure modes and no marked middle.

beats.act: ACT 2 — chapter five: the accuracy dial
beats.role_note: Carried verbatim from claude-cli-rag-vector-databases B08. Caption reworded only to name the Chapter 5 build; every point is unchanged.
beats.narration_text: Chapter five: searching a hundred thousand vectors. Exact search never misses and does not scale, so you approximate — and the approximation is literally a dial. Compare a third of one percent of the collection, and you get a third of the true neighbours back. Compare ten percent, and you get ninety-six. You pick the point on that curve.

beats.act: ACT 3 — chapter six: no method wins everything
beats.role_note: Carried from claude-cli-rag-retrieval-methods B07. Caption reworded only to name the Chapter 6 build.
beats.narration_text: Chapter six: which kind of match. Sparse matches literal words, and won an exact policy code. Dense matches meaning, and won the paraphrase. And the hybrid — the combination that is supposed to be the safe default — is the one that missed. Only plain dense retrieval got both queries right.

shot.visual_intent: the three-by-two method/query matrix with the surprising hybrid miss as the one accent — carried over from the Chapter 6 reel

sparse row resolves — HIT, MISS
dense row resolves — HIT, HIT, YES
hybrid row resolves — HIT, then the accented MISS

props.headline: Only One Method Got Both.
props.caption: Top-1 on the gold passage, measured by the Chapter 6 build's hybrid_search.py over 12 passages. The hybrid miss is the surprise.

beats.act: ACT 3b — the kicker: how the default lost
beats.role_note: Carried verbatim from claude-cli-rag-retrieval-methods B08. The single most concrete evidence for the reel's whole claim.
beats.narration_text: And here is how it lost. Fusion sums one over sixty plus each rank. The wrong passage was sparse's confident number one; the right one was only sparse's third. Point zero three two five two, against point zero three two two seven. A quarter of one thousandth decided it. The fusion counted ranks. It never reasoned about either list.

shot.visual_intent: the two candidates' rank contributions written out as reciprocals and summed, with the correct answer that lost marked in terracotta — carried over from the Chapter 6 reel

TR-114 row in terracotta: sparse #3 + dense #1 → 0.03227
the margin settles beneath: 0.00025 apart

remotion.note: reused verbatim from claude-cli-rag-retrieval-methods B08 (props-only reuse)

props.headline: Outvoted By A Quarter Of A Thousandth.
props.query: Does the company help pay for grad school?
props.marginLabel: 0.00025 apart — the wrong passage wins the fusion
props.caption: RRF sums 1/(k + rank) across both lists. It has no way to know that sparse was confidently wrong.

beats.role_note: NO-SOURCE-NO-VERDICT — every line traces to one of the three source reels.
beats.narration_text: Let's recap. Chapter four: where you cut decides what can be found, and there is no universally correct size. Chapter five: approximate search trades recall for speed, and the trade is a number you set. Chapter six: sparse and dense fail on different queries, and combining them usually helps — but this run was one of the times it did not. Three layers, three tradeoffs, and not one of them ships with a default you can install and forget.

artifactLines: Ch. 4 — Chunking: where you cut decides what retrieval can find. Too small loses context, too large loses precision, and no size is universally correct.
Ch. 5 — Indexing: exact search doesn't scale, so you approximate. Recall for speed is an explicit dial — 0.3% of the collection bought 33% recall, 10.2% bought 96%.
Ch. 6 — Matching: sparse won an exact code, dense won the paraphrase, and the hybrid missed one by 0.00025. Fusion counts ranks; it doesn't reason.
The through-line: every layer is a setting, and the only way to know yours is to measure it on your own data.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — read aloud verbatim, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'Here are the three retrieval decisions I've made by default — my chunk size, my index's accuracy setting, and my choice of retriever. For each one, tell me what measurement would prove it wrong on my data, and what the cheapest version of that measurement looks like.' The second half is the part that earns its keep. Anything will hand you best practices; asking what would falsify each choice, and what the cheap version of that test costs, is what turns three inherited defaults into three decisions you can actually defend.
